abstract: AAA+ (ATPases Associated with diverse cellular Activities) motors harness ATP hydrolysis to remodel substrates, often through a spiral staircase architecture which is commonly associated with a sequential "hand-over-hand" translocation mechanism. However, the extent to which motor activity requires strict sequential order and interprotomer coordination remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigate the functional resilience of an archaeal AAA+ unfoldase, VAT, using reconstituted heterohexamers containing wild-type protomers and variants defective in nucleotide binding, hydrolysis, substrate engagement, or regulatory control. Quantitative modeling of steady-state ATPase activity and substrate unfolding reveals motif-dependent partial cooperativity. ATP hydrolysis is best described by local interprotomer coupling, whereas substrate unfolding exhibits a threshold-dependent response to defects in conserved mechanochemical motifs. Walker A and Arginine-finger lesions inhibit neighboring ATPase activity but are partially tolerated during unfolding. Pore-loop mutations stimulate ATP turnover while more strongly impairing unfolding. In contrast, N-terminal domain-mediated autoinhibition follows an independent model in both assays, consistent with controlling catalytic output predominantly at the individual protomer level while preserving interprotomer coordination for function. Together, these findings reveal that ATP turnover and substrate unfolding respond differently to local perturbations, with tolerance to protomer defects determined by the mechanochemical element affected. This motif-dependent resilience highlights the operational plasticity of an AAA+ ring and challenges strictly sequential models in which a single defective protomer arrests the motor.
